sense: the greatest or the farthest: utmost, outermost

evidence: Cic. Off. 1.33: summum jūs summa injūria
Cic. Rep. 1.1: ad summam senectūtem, to extreme old age (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: The utmost degree of a thing: the greatest danger, extreme old age, summā vōce, at the top of one’s voice. Its first sense is the top of a thing (summus mōns, the mountain top).

At the far edge or the end: the farthest borders, the last day (Lewis & Short: “the outermost, utmost, extreme, so most freq.”); and so the last resort, the extreme case. Lewis & Short notes that extrēmus is not compared in classical Latin.
The farthest away, or the last in a series; less often of degree than summus.

phrases.latin: Majōrī tamen partī placuit, hōc reservātō ad extrēmum cāsum cōnsiliō interim reī ēventum experīrī et castra dēfendere.
phrases.english: But most of them decided to keep this plan as a last resort, and meanwhile to wait and see how things turned out and defend the camp.

phrases.latin: sīve in extrēmōs penetrābit Indōs … sīve trāns altās gradiētur Alpēs
phrases.english: whether he will make his way to the farthest Indians … or march across the high Alps
